World.title: In praise of Mymensingh’s Bangla folk ballads
World.content:
Folk-ballads are living archives that represent the imagination, values, ideas, and aesthetics of the people to whom they belong. Bangla literature has a rich repertoire of folk ballads. We are, however, quite oblivious of this treasure trove and, therefore, there is a dearth of research on these folk elements.

Czech Indologist Dusan Zbavitel's Bengali Folk-Ballads From Mymensingh And The Problem Of Their Authenticity can be called a wonderful exception in this regard. It is considered to be the first literary study of the beautiful folk-ballads from Mymensingh. The study was published by the University of Calcutta in 1963.

A brief background of the book may not be irrelevant here. In 1923, Rai Bahadur Dineshchandra Sen edited a volume of epic songs from the Mymensingh District of the then Eastern Bengal under the title Maimansimha-gitika. The ballads were mainly collected by Chandra Kumar De, a literary activist from the area. In the following years, Dineshchandra published three more volumes of balladic texts containing epic songs from different parts of Eastern Bengal. The beautiful ballads received enthusiastic response and admiration in India and abroad. However, for some scholars these ballads were too good, and they shared doubts about the ‍antiquity, authenticity and folk character of these lores. Dusan Zbavitel found this uncertainty "highly regrettable" and undertook a study to assign to the ballads their proper place—"one of the high points of Bengali literature". Dr Zbavitel tried to find out: "what is it that makes them so excellent?"

Zbavitel confined his analysis to the study of the ballads originating in Mymensingh—41 ballads containing more than 21,000 verses. He took an arduous effort of analysing each of these 41 ballads to prove their originality and, I must say, he achieved his goal with marked success.

One key argument put forward by Zbavitel in favour of the originality of the gitikas from Mymensingh is that these ballads are not collected by a single person and, still, there are similarities among the ballads: identical images, and similar artistic approach and common inventory of similes and metaphors. So these ballads couldn't be the creation of a modern poet as suggested by some detractors.

According to Zbavitel, the most significant aspect of these folk ballads is that they are devoid of any religious implications. They generally show harmonious co-existence of the Hindu and Muslim communities, without religious bias on either side. Zbavitel points out the fact that most of the Hindu ballads were collected from Muslim singers, which shows, according to him, that these folk poems were enjoyed and appreciated by both the communities with the same eagerness. The secular outlook of the folk ballads is diametrically opposite to the explicit religious connotation of the classical Bangla literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas and Vaisnava literature.

Zbavitel extensively discusses the ideological and artistic approach of the ballad writers, verse and rhyme technique, and use of similes and metaphors in chapter three and four of the book. The most dominant motif, according to Zbavitel, is love. Even the historical and heroic epics can be grouped into this category.

As to the literary techniques, the ballad writers, being true to the characteristics of folk epics, do not try to introduce innovations in their lyrical dictions. They are content with the poetic means offered by their predecessors. They want to tell an interesting and touching story in a simple garb, fresh with country scenes and feelings.

Zbavitel also discusses the manner of preservation of the folk ballads—preserved, in most cases, in torsos. Referring to two versions of the same ballad, Maishal Bandhu, he argues, "The 'original' ballads [were] sometimes rewritten by another folk poet, or other poets, quite freely, without any scruples; whole portions, as well as individual couplets and verses, were taken over, others were replaced by newly replaced passages, and the story itself was often changed." The reasons behind such changes, according to Zbavitel, might be an effort to offer listeners a 'better' story than the original one.

Due to this oral nature of preservation, it is always difficult to prove the originality of folk elements. If we undertake an effort to study the folklore of Bangladesh, Zbavitel's book will be an invaluable companion guide.

Rabindranath Tagore wrote to Dinesh Chandra Sen in appreciation of the book Maimansimha-gitika, "Classical Bengali literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas are ponds dug on by order and at the expense of the rich, but Maimansimha-gitika is a source of exuberance from the deepest level of the heart of rural Bengal, a clear stream of genuine pain. There has never been such a creation of self-forgetting rasa [aesthetic joy] in Bengali literature." [translation by the author]

While celebrating the Bengali new year this Pohela Boishakh, may we remember the melody and the essence of communal harmony embedded in Maimansimha-gitika.

Shamsuddoza Sajen is a journalist and researcher. He can be contacted at [email protected].

World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: 'This is now terminal': UK braces for prospect of sixth PM in seven years
World.content:
A sixth prime minister in seven years — it was an unimaginable prospect not so long ago, but now, some experts are describing it as an inevitability facing Britain.

Sir Keir Starmer, who led Labour to a landslide general election victory in July 2024, has become so unpopular that even some colleagues are framing his demise as a case of not if, but when.

This week has been another shocker for the PM, who has been trying to explain how Peter Mandelson — a Labour kingmaker and friend of the child sex offender Jeffrey Epstein — ended up as the United Kingdom's ambassador to the US.

Critics have been calling on Sir Keir to resign for months, but on Wednesday, Labour MP Jonathan Brash added his voice to the growing chorus.

He used an interview on British television network GB News to rail about the PM's leadership, saying he was "fed up" with the "psychodrama in Westminster".

"I mean, ultimately, we're in a situation now where I don't think anyone reasonably expects the prime minister to lead the party into the next election," he said.

Mr Brash's time frame is generous. The next general election is not due to be held in the UK until 2029.

There are 411 Labour MPs in the lower house of the British parliament, and the odd vent from a backbencher is unlikely to worry Sir Keir's team. But it does show the PM is facing increasing criticisms, including from his own side of the chamber.

Donald Trump shakes hands with Peter Mandelson in the Oval Office last year. (Reuters: Leah Millis)

Sir Keir, already struggling in the polls when the Mandelson saga began several months ago, appears set to be undone by the appointment.

"I think this is now terminal for Keir Starmer," Dan Hodges, a veteran political columnist for The Mail on Sunday, told the ABC. "He was in a very difficult political situation before the Peter Mandelson crisis broke.

"He was already very, very unpopular in the country. The Peter Mandelson affair has further undermined his authority."

Mandelson, who has held multiple powerful roles during his long career, has towered over the Labour Party for decades.

Until recently, he had been renowned as one of the UK's most effective political operators. But he was never far from controversy. He twice resigned from the cabinet during his 12 years as an MP. An unflattering nickname, the Prince of Darkness, might offer clues as to his style.

Mandelson was dismissed as ambassador to the US in September last year, after making multiple appearances in the Epstein files. He held the post in Washington for just seven months.

His sacking was, in hindsight, closer to the beginning of this scandal than the end. Lately, UK political discourse has focused on whether Sir Keir knew the 72-year-old had failed the necessary security checks to take up the role.

What the PM and his office were aware of in relation to that depends on who you ask.

Sir Keir has been in the House of Commons this week, claiming he was "furious" about the whole affair. Critics argue he should have known better than to sign off on someone with Mandelson's history.

A parliamentary inquiry into the appointment has been ensuring the story stays in the headlines. On Tuesday, the former head of the UK's foreign office, Sir Olly Robbins, gave evidence that has been described as "explosive".

Next week, Sir Keir's former chief of staff, Morgan McSweeney, will testify. He is often characterised as the architect of Mandelson's appointment.

Starmer 'one of the few grown-ups on world stage'

Not everyone believes the PM is doomed.

Tom Baldwin, a former senior Labour advisor and Sir Keir's biographer, told the ABC that while the leader was under pressure, his fate was not sealed.

"These things turn around very, very fast and anyone making predictions in the current atmosphere is a fool, I don't want to be one of them," he said.

Baldwin said "it would be bad for the British government" if Sir Keir was removed.

"I think that it would be inward-looking when the government needs to be outward-looking," he said.

"I think also it would be bad for the country. It's a really dangerous time for Britain and the world, and Keir Starmer is one of the few grown-ups on the world stage. I think he'd be a great loss."

Things are likely to get worse for the PM next month, however.

Many analysts now believe Sir Keir will be ousted sometime after May 7, when a series of council elections will be held around Britain.

In the UK, national political parties dominate local government, and Labour is expected to lose control of multiple municipalities when people head to the polls. If the results go as expected, Sir Keir's opponents will couch them as a referendum on his leadership.

"I think he'll survive up until the local elections, but once they're out of the way, I think at that point the Labour Party will start looking for a new leader and a new prime minister," Hodges said.

Opponents are already capitalising on the PM's deteriorating position. In parliament on Monday, Sir Ed Davey, leader of the centrist Liberal Democrats party, said Sir Keir "gives every impression of a prime minister in office, but not in power".

Keir Starmer is a prominent figure on the world stage, but deeply unpopular among UK voters. (Pool: Jonathan Brady via Reuters)

While there are multiple candidates, an obvious Labour successor to Sir Keir is yet to emerge.

Polarising former deputy PM Angela Rayner is facing an investigation into her tax affairs, which would need to be concluded before any tilt. Health Secretary Wes Streeting — a Mandelson protege — and former leader Ed Miliband have also been touted as options, among several other ministers.

Manchester's Labour Mayor Andy Burnham has supporters, but no seat in parliament — something that would need to change for him to stand.

"Australians know the futility of constantly changing leader to try to curry favour with the voters. What you need to do is change to face them," John McTernan, an advisor to former British PM Tony Blair, told ABC News Breakfast this week.

"So the Labour Party needs to know how it should change to attract voters back again before it even thinks about a leadership contest.

" But leadership speculation is going on at the moment, the elections in May will crystallise that and sometime during this year it's likely there will be a challenge to Sir Keir Starmer. "

On May 13, King Charles III will officially open a new parliamentary sitting year. As per British traditions, the monarch will announce the government's priorities for the months ahead.

That legislative agenda will be followed by a debate and vote among MPs — a process which could reveal how much support the PM has.

Sir Keir came to power in 2024 promising an end to government "chaos", that had seen the Conservative Party churn through multiple prime ministers, including one — Liz Truss — who lasted just 49 days.

Less than two years later, many people now believe he is set to join the people he ran against on Britain's political scrap heap.

World.title: It's a very bad time to be a baby boomer, politically speaking
World.content:
Politically, it's a very bad time to be a baby boomer.

It is not just that intergenerational equity has become, rightly, a priority for Labor.

It's also that this government, which always has an ear cocked to public opinion, is fully aware of the resentment towards boomers from many people aged 25–45 who see themselves paying for their elders while often unable to afford the housing that was more readily available to a "lucky" generation.

When on Wednesday Health Minister Mark Butler announced the government would scrap the top-up private health insurance subsidy for those over 65, brought in by John Howard, he cast the decision in generational equity terms.

The extra subsidy "means two households on the same income receive different levels of government support, based only on their age," Butler said. "That's not fair between generations."

Removal of this (income-tested) benefit will save the government $3 billion over the forward estimates. With an aging population putting an increasing burden on the budget, the government is repurposing this money into aged care, including paying the full cost of showering for those on home care packages. (So, the government might argue, there are swings and roundabouts for boomers.)

Treasurer Jim Chalmers will make intergenerational equity a major thread woven through his May 12 budget.

The politics says housing unaffordability remains red hot among voters. It is now accepted the capital gains discount will be hit; also, negative gearing is likely to be altered.

Other sweeteners in the tax or housing areas are possible — if they come they would have, at least in part, an intergenerational equity lens.

Loading...

First target, the NDIS

The government is under pressure not to splurge in the budget, not least because the Reserve Bank will be watching closely. But Butler's announcement of a "reset" of the National Disability Insurance Scheme has given Chalmers some funds to play with.

The estimated savings from the NDIS overhaul are huge: $22 billion over a four-year budget period.

The government is absolutely right to tackle the NDIS's multiple problems. Despite initial curbs in Labor's first term, when Bill Shorten was its minister, the expenditure trajectory was still unsustainable.

ABC Politics in your inbox Sign up to the ABC Politics newsletter with Courtney Gould

But achieving the projected savings will be a herculean endeavour. The states will drag their feet and drive hard bargains. Much detail hasn't been worked out, and discussions with stakeholders will be difficult. Stories of people thrown off the scheme by the cuts will abound. The program's new rate of cost growth will be only 2 per cent annually in the next four years — a big cut in real terms.

But much of the pain will be delayed until long after this budget. And getting the NDIS announcement out now means Chalmers' budget night can concentrate on the good news.

Early signs are the opposition will back the thrust of the changes (while noting that when the Morrison government tried to make some reforms, they were demonised by the then Labor opposition).

As the government puts together its budget — with the prime minister saying "resilience" will be at its centre — the context is dominated by the Middle East conflict and the alarming prospects for fuel supplies if the situation is not resolved soon.

Gas under pressure

The government is now confronted with a campaign, that has considerable community support, for a new tax to be imposed on gas exports, as companies stand to benefit from the higher prices brought by the international crisis.

This week the battle over the tax was ventilated in often heated hearings at a Senate inquiry, chaired by the Greens, which will report before the budget.

One of those arguing for a new tax is Ken Henry, formerly head of treasury, who chaired the far-reaching tax inquiry commissioned by the Rudd government (which recommended a mining super profits tax).

In his submission to the Senate inquiry, Henry dwelt on generational equity. Canvassing how the proceeds of a gas tax could be used, he said, "Consideration might be given to three dimensions: public debt management, nature repair, and boosting productivity.

"All three dimensions are highly significant for the living standards of future generations and thus offer the opportunity to address sources of intergenerational inequity.

"Revenue raised from a windfall gains tax could be invested in a sovereign wealth fund for the benefit of future generations."

While that thinking would fit naturally with the inclination of Chalmers, other considerations are pushing against the government going down this path.

These include warnings about the potential disincentive for investment coming from the companies, which have an advertising campaign running, and from countries that take our gas.

Loading

Tax not likely

In his recent "fuel diplomacy" trips to Singapore, Brunei and Malaysia, Anthony Albanese's mantra was that Australia is a dependable supplier of LNG.

His messaging has flagged that he is disinclined to the tax. In a podcast this week with The Daily Aus, Albanese rejected the suggestion the companies were paying little tax.



"Some of the facts haven't been out there," Albanese said. "The truth is that the gas taxes in the last financial year […] were around about $22 billion. So, I've seen there are reports suggesting that there's more on beer tax than gas. It's just not true." Pressed for detail, he pointed out the Petroleum Resource Rent Tax was not the only relevant tax — the gas producers also paid company tax.

Albanese said he understood people would like to see more taxes paid. "In budgets, we look at the full suite of measures. What I am saying very clearly though is that we honour contracts and we honour those arrangements with countries."

Resources Minister Madeleine King is cautious with her words but is obviously against a new tax.

Perhaps more important is what Western Australian Premier Roger Cook said this week, when he opposed a new gas tax. "I don't think it'd be good for Western Australia and I've made those views clear to the prime minister," he said. Cook's views hold a lot of sway with Albanese.

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi will visit Australia in early May, just before the budget. She is likely to get reassurance there will be no new gas tax.

Michelle Grattan is a professorial fellow at the University of Canberra and chief political correspondent at The Conversation, where this article first appeared.

World.title: Plan to end NDIS 'wild west' will flip rules on their head for providers
World.content:
A plan to recover as much as $4.6 billion a year going out the door of the National Disability Insurance Scheme to criminal fraud, inflated invoices and incorrect payments could wipe out many NDIS providers unable to afford the costs of stricter compliance, the sector warns.

NDIS Minister Mark Butler has announced reforms that will flip the current disability scheme on its head, reversing a trend where most support providers are unregistered and the agency has little visibility over most claims to one where claims must be proven before they are paid, and most providers must prove they have the necessary skills and business practices to offer services.

And the rules for what providers can charge will also be tightened, with providers made to register if they want to charge a higher rate, and Mr Butler granted ultimate price setting power, akin to rules for the aged care sector.

Accidental fraud, and deliberate exploitation

The National Disability Insurance Agency estimates 6 to 10 per cent of payments made to participants are lost to inflated invoices, organised crime or ineligible payments each year, or about $2.8 billion to $4.6 billion.

On average, it equates to as much as $6,500 in payments per NDIS participant.

How did the NDIS get so expensive? With more changes surrounding the NDIS just announced, here's everything you need to know about the scheme.

The Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission has said the scale of integrity issues inside the NDIS extends beyond "isolated or opportunistic" misuse and includes deliberate fraud and organised exploitation consistent with the behaviour of serious organised crime groups.

"In more serious cases, collusive arrangements have been identified between providers and participants, nominees or family members, including the provision of cash or other inducements to facilitate fraudulent access to the NDIS or ongoing misuse of participant plans," the ACIC wrote in a recent Senate inquiry submission.

"A central enabling methodology is the use of cash incentives, or 'kickbacks', to participants, nominees or family members. These arrangements operate along a spectrum ranging from knowing collusion to coercion, and the ACIC assesses that some participants are likely unaware they are involved in fraudulent activity."

Just on Thursday, Australian Federal Police charged a 33-year-old Sydney man over $1.5 million in claims for NDIS services which were not provided, alleging he was also suspected to be associated with organised criminal groups.

Police allegedly linked the man to 80 NDIS claims submitted against 22 "unknowing" participants in early 2024.

Police allege one man fraudulently claimed $1.5 million worth of NDIS services not provided from 22 "unknowing" participants. (Australian Federal Police)

Mr Butler said cleaning up "rorts" was not just about saving the federal government money, but about improving what participants got out of their set budgets.

"Every dollar that is skimmed off a participant's plan by a dodgy provider is a dollar that doesn't go to their support or their service," Mr Butler told the Guardian.

End to 'let it rip' NDIS provider market

But Mr Butler conceded on Wednesday that the government's reforms last term and nearly half a billion dollars spent to crack down on fraud through enhancing detection and payment auditing had failed to rein in the scheme's $50 billion a year costs.

"Measures we've introduced to control spending are simply not working as we intended," Mr Butler told the National Press Club.

The minister has now announced plans to end what he called a "let it rip" market of NDIS service providers to a more tightly regulated scheme that offered less choice, but better quality control and oversight.

Mark Butler has announced several changes to improve the quality of services available to NDIS participants, while seeking to rein in ballooning costs of the scheme. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

The current market of more than 1,400 plan managers, who handle the financial administration of a participant's plan, will be replaced with a panel of approved providers who rather than charging fees to process invoices or manage an individual budget could instead receive block funding and grants to provide more generalised services.

The additional layer of quality control over plan managers would also curb what criminal intelligence has identified as cases of collusion or "conflicts of interest", where a plan manager directs a participant's funding to businesses they stand to gain from, including their own or a friend's.

The government hopes by lifting the bar for who is approved to manage NDIS plans it will also end a practice of one in five plans being subject to an unscheduled reassessment — often at the request of plan managers — which leads to an average 20 per cent increase in the plan's value.

Mr Butler said the government's reforms would reduce spending in this area by about a third.

Disability Intermediaries Australia acting chief executive Tanya Walford said the government must provide more clarity of how the transition would happen.

"We really want to make sure we support the workforce that is in it for the right reasons, to actually transition into a vibrant choice-driven, participant-driven NDIS," Ms Walford said.

"We need to see the detail and want to work with the agency to make sure whatever happens next is fair and equitable for people who have spent their lives building up a business as well as participants who are receiving a service ... and of course the taxpayer."

Disability community surprised by scale of planned NDIS cuts NDIS Minister Mark Butler has defended the government's latest cost-cutting changes to the scheme in an interview with the ABC, amid an avalanche of participant concern.

New requirements for mandatory registration of businesses providing support workers, daily living supports, personal supports and other higher risk activities will also weed out some unscrupulous providers — though the industry fears it could drive out many small businesses and sole traders who operate legitimately but cannot afford the process to become registered.

Registering requires providers to pass an audit showing they meet a series of standards, including that they have acceptable procedures to manage incidents and complaints, suitable qualifications, conflict of interest policies, and are able to reliably provide day-to-day operations.

Mr Butler said the market established a decade ago, which had few controls in order to avoid suppressing a nascent care industry, was "unlike any other market we have in a social program".

"We've got a whole lot of people … who were working in other industries, who decided to leave those industries and instead become part of the NDIS, not with any qualifications or background in disability services," he said on Thursday.

"We've got a high degree of variability within the NDIS market between people who have a lot of experience, a lot of qualifications in disability services, alongside people who frankly don't have much. And they're all charging the same.

"We want to see more quality, more confidence for participants that when they're engaging a provider to give them some service, that provider has been vetted, that they can be confident they've got the right qualifications, the right character, that the money is going to the right place."

'Huge' cost of registration could drive away good providers

But Professionals Australia chief executive Sam Roberts, who represents NDIS allied health workers, said the sweeping reforms announced yesterday to save $35 billion over four years were "appalling".

"It's just targeting disabled people and targeting the people who work for them, calling them fraudsters. It's just appalling," Mr Roberts said.

"Fraud needs to be removed and kicked out. [But] with a scheme of this size ... there are examples of fraud. When you're spending half a billion dollars on getting rid of fraud, you are going to find examples of fraud."

Mr Roberts said the current registration scheme was "broken", taking workers sometimes 18 months or more to become registered, at a cost of thousands of dollars.

"For workers to get registration costs them $1,000 to $3,000 to pay to go get registered, then to fill out all the paperwork, which is quite complicated, there is a whole cottage industry which has been created which charges people thousands of dollars to get the paperwork ready," he said.

"If you're needing a certification audit it will [also] cost you somewhere between $3,000 to $12,000."

Mr Roberts said those costs would drive providers forced to register away from the scheme, leaving more service gaps.

Inclusion Australia chief executive Maeve Kennedy said the organisation supported a universal registration scheme.

"However it's essential that stronger oversight needs to improve safety without reducing choice," Ms Kennedy said.

Ms Kennedy highlighted the complexities of registering providers in some cases, such as where a person with complex support needs who has limited suitable options establishes a "service-for-one", with family directly employing staff and taking responsibility for business processes.

"Support workers in those cohort are generally really highly trained ... and they are trained in supporting the particular individual, recognising communication, recognising behaviours. It's really highly skilled but a lot of those workers at the moment are unregistered," Ms Kennedy said.

"Any changes that are really sudden ... cause a lot of fear. But we don't think the government is intending sudden changes."

Ms Kennedy agreed that costs to register were a "huge" barrier, and the one-size-fits all approach to registration did not account for low, medium and high risk supports.

The government has flagged it intends to introduce a graduated, risk-based registration scheme.

End to NDIS payment claims 'on serviettes'

Alongside registration, the government will reverse the onus for providers receiving taxpayer funding, from a scheme where providers receive money and then provide evidence of how it has been spent to one where providers must first submit a claim before receiving funds.

Mark Woodland, founder of healthcare software company Kismet, said that would incentivise those hoping to be paid to correctly submit claims.

"You're front-loading the admin and the incentive onto the allied health provider who wants to be paid, compared to this third-party, like a support coordinator, checking an invoice that has been sent through the post," Mr Woodland said.

"I would argue a lot of it is accidental — wrong business name, wrong amount, you've missed a decimal point ... the majority is just errors, mistakes. That is what you wipe out."

A new digital payments system will end a long-outdated culture of handwritten invoices, which Mr Woodland said were often missing information, written on "serviettes" and could not be cross-checked with tax office or business watchdog data to automatically flag suspicious activity.

But Mr Woodland said he expected the path to restore trust would be a "long journey".

"Restoration of trust almost takes longer than it was to break it. If you broke trust over ten years, it's going to take 20 years to restore that trust," he said.

"What I did like about the announcement yesterday from the minister is at least we're doing something."

World.title: The NDIS gave participants their lives back. Now they fear what's to come
World.content:
Do you remember a moment that changed your life?

For hundreds of thousands of people, that moment was the day they became a participant of the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS).

Before Robin Eames became a participant, they were housebound and relying on housemates to act as informal support workers.

"That was damaging to me and those relationships," says Eames, who lives with multiple disabilities, including autism and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

NDIS-funded exercise physiology and hydrotherapies helped strengthen their body, support workers enabled them to complete personal care tasks, and a new wheelchair made the outside world more accessible than ever before.

Robin Eames says the NDIS changed their life. (ABC News: Chris Taylor)

But Eames is now one of hundreds of thousands of participants who no longer know what the future holds after the Albanese government unveiled a dramatic new suite of cost cutting changes this week.

Those changes include a new eligibility process and cutting about 160,000 people from the now-$50 billion scheme to put the brakes on its "runaway" growth.

It is not entirely clear yet which participants will be removed from the scheme, but Health Minister Mark Butler says it will not start until the government is confident "there are other systems of support in place".

NDIS figures at a glance The NDIS now supports more than 760,000 participants, close to double the original estimate

Spending has been projected to reach $53.4 billion this year, close to the $59 billion for defence

The government projects the latest suite of changes could save $22 billion over the next four years

The scheme is growing at 10.3 per cent per year, down from more than 22 per cent under the Coalition, but still making it the second fastest growing form of federal expenditure

The government wants annual growth at around 5-6 per cent

Even before this week's announcement, distressed participants were writing to us each week reporting sudden cuts to their plans.

Many accepted the scheme needed reform and were bracing for significant change, but they were not expecting the government's announcement to go as far as it did.

Eames says the news, and the accompanying lack of immediate detail, made their "stomach drop".

"I'm worried they're going to cut my funding and that I may lose access [to the scheme] entirely," they said.

" The NDIS gave me my life back and I'm concerned it's now getting taken away. "

'What's the point of getting up if you have nowhere to go?'

The whiplash for participants is stark.

They set up their lives around NDIS rules. But now the rules have changed, things they have become used to are being taken away — or are at much higher risk of being removed.

Some things that they were able to have funded in the past — such as sex workers or equine therapy — have not passed the pub test.

These services were far from common, but taxpayers are asking why they were allowed in the first place.

But they were, primarily thanks to a lack of guardrails from successive governments as the scheme was set up.

Eames says participants have done nothing wrong and that the failures of others have led to this dramatic financial intervention, which feels "punitive".

"It feels like we're being treated as burdens and scammers when we're just trying to lead our lives. Everyone deserves the chance at a good life and a happy future," they said.

A key pillar of the next set of changes is cutting social and community participation supports, which includes the funding of support workers to take participants to appointments, work and social activities.

This category accounts for more than a fifth of all spending on the NDIS, and the government hopes reducing the average spend per person from $33,000 to $26,000 will help it achieve a sizeable chunk of its overall savings.

Jarrod Sandell-Hay says social and community participation supports are not frivolous. (ABC News: Patrick Stone)

People with Disability Australia vice-president Jarrod Sandell-Hay is an NDIS participant who lives with cerebral palsy.

The wheelchair user relies on social and community participation supports to go to the GP, head to work and get food at the supermarket to feed his family.

"It's really important disabled people are in the community, they're seen, they contribute," Mr Sandell-Hay says.

"The idea that we're just having coffee and going to the movies, even though that's important too, that's not all we're doing. We're fathers, we're mothers, we're brothers and we're sisters.

" What's the point of getting out of bed if you have nowhere to go? "

Jarrod Sandell-Hay is among the many participants concerned about the cuts. (ABC News: Patrick Stone)

The government says it will set up a $200 million Inclusive Communities Fund for community organisations to provide similar services for less money.

Mr Sandell-Hay says it is critical those services do not just turn into "day groups" in which people with disability "are put into a room together".

He says losing his community participation supports would limit his ability to work.

"That means taxpayers would be paying for someone who is not contributing as much as he could," Mr Sandell-Hay says.

Fear of the unknowns

Taxpayers deserve to know that their contributions to the country's fastest-growing social government program are being used as efficiently as possible.

It has become clear over the last few years that has not been happening.

While participants and their families are feeling the heat, the status quo was untenable.

"We can't afford for the NDIS to continue growing at its present rate … but, far more importantly, we can't afford for the NDIS to fail," Mr Butler said on Wednesday.

Mr Sandell-Hay says no-one wants the NDIS to succeed more than participants and their families.

The government says it will take its next steps in partnership with the disability community and the states and territories, which will have to step up to ensure nobody with disability falls between the cracks.

That is easier said than done, though — tensions are already flaring and early signs suggest the politics are far from finished.

World.title: Charts explain why fertiliser prices aren't coming down anytime soon
World.content:
Fertiliser prices will continue to rise for months to come and even an immediate opening of the Strait of Hormuz will do little to anchor them, according to analysts at CRU Group.

Loading...

Fertiliser is an essential farming input, relied on by food producers across the globe.

Prices have been skyrocketing since the months-long US-Israeli war in Iran led to a near-complete standstill of maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.

It's all taking place when Australian farmers need fertiliser the most, when they're sowing their winter crops.

Fertilisers, put simply and very broadly, provide plants with nitrogen, commonly via urea or potassium in the form of potash.

Others, such as Monoammonium phosphate (MAP) and Di-ammonium Phosphate (DAP) provide plants with a mix of phosphorous and nitrogen.

Supplies constrained

This chart shows how much fertiliser Middle Eastern producers exported last year.

It is expressed as a percentage of global exports and broken down into regions: Iran, Israel, those impacted by shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz and those at risk in the broader region: Egypt, Syria, Jordan and Oman.

A significant volume of urea and phosphate fertiliser production needs to be exported through the Strait of Hormuz.

But it's important to pay attention to sulphur too - it is an important ingredient in fertiliser manufacturing, as well as mining and industrial processes.

In March, Iranian strikes on Qatari energy facilities led to the shutdown of QAFCO's Mesaieed urea plant, one of the largest production facilities in the world.

Iranian fertiliser plants have been impacted by strikes on South Pas gas field.

Missing ingredient

Sulphur is a critical ingredient in fertiliser manufacturing and it's also a by-product of oil and gas production, so the Middle East is a dominant supplier.

In its most simple terms, dissolving phosphate rock in sulphuric acid makes the phosphate available for plants.

So higher sulphur prices make phosphate fertilisers more expensive.

China is a big producer of phosphate fertilisers, but it has had export restrictions in place since last year.

Each year, Chinese producers usually export phosphate fertilisers in a window between November and March.

Last year, exports did not start until the middle of June, and export volumes hit a 12-year low.

Rising sulphur prices have led fertiliser market analysts to forecast an even smaller export season this year.

Price responses

This chart compared a set of fertiliser prices with a set of grain prices to create a measure of affordability over time.

Higher values indicate fertiliser is becoming more expensive.

There have been price spikes in this market before, most notably in 2007/08 and after Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022.

But Russia-Ukraine war also sent grain prices higher, and Middle Eastern production was not affected, so Australian farmers weren't in the same position they are now.

Urea production

Urea is the most-used fertiliser around the world.

CRU Group estimates 1.9 million tonnes of production have been taken out of the market by disruptions to energy infrastructure and manufacturing plants across the Middle East.

When you break out urea from the broader category of fertilisers in the affordability chart above, the picture is grim.

Urea is at its most unaffordable since the index started and competition is stiff on the international market.

Stiff competition

India and Australia are paying some of the highest prices for fertiliser in the market.

Last week, Indian Potash Limited (IPL) issued tenders to secure 2.5 million tonnes of urea.

According to Reuters, the lowest bids came in about US$935/t (A$1,306) and most bids clustered around US$1,000/t (A$1,397) and climbed as high as US$1,136/t (A$1,587).

In comparison, West Australian farmers are already similar prices, according to president of WAFarmers grains council Mark Fowler.

"At the moment, urea is around $1430-$1470/t, that is my understanding," Mr Fowler told the WA Country Hour on Wednesday.

Australia recently inked a deal with Indonesia which will result in Incitec Pivot importing 250,000 tonnes of urea, around one-fifth of what Australian farmers usually apply to their crops each year.

Julie Collins says the government is working to head off a fertiliser shortfall later in the year. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Earlier this week, the federal government said it would underwrite further shipments made by Incitec Pivot and CSBP to secure additional supplies farmers would need in the middle of the year.

"We certainly have a shortfall … but what we're doing is we're out sourcing more fertiliser right across the globe," said Agriculture Minister Julie Collins.

The federal government has also lowered the biosecurity requirements for fertiliser imports.

"Outside of government to government deals, I think Australia will continue to look for supplies from regions it may not have sought them before in the absence of the Middle East like Nigeria and Oman," said CRU senior nitrogen analyst Lewis Walters.

World.title: Viva boss tells Kohler more refineries needed for secure fuel supply
World.content:
Viva Energy boss Scott Wyatt recalls he was on the phone with the fuel refinery's general manager when disaster struck late at night last Wednesday.

"We were working through the final details of the cargoes for the first two cargoes the government was asking us to acquire on their behalf," Mr Wyatt told Alan Kohler's That's Business podcast.

" And obviously at that point shortly after 11:15pm the call came through … about the fire at the refinery. "

The fire at one of the two remaining oil refineries in Australia raged for more than 12 hours.

Scott Wyatt says the fire will not cause any long-term damage to output. (ABC News: Simon Tucci)

By the time it was extinguished, the flames had left Geelong's Viva Energy site looking like a "war zone", one bystander noted.

Up to 50 staff were working when the blaze broke out.

All escaped unharmed, but nearby residents were ordered to shelter indoors as firefighters worked to tame the fire.

"I got in the car and drove to the site," Mr Wyatt said.

"I got there about 3 o'clock [in the morning] and then … obviously, by that stage, the response teams were all in place, the incident was being managed, and you know, as you need to do at that point, is obviously start preparing … communications and starting to engage stakeholders."

A witness described the Geelong refinery fire as loud, creating a type of sucking noise. (Supplied: Ben Young)

Mr Wyatt described the response to the fire as "textbook", but said he would not know "for some time" what caused the fire.

The blaze at the refinery, which is 500 metres from the nearest residential area, was finally extinguished at around noon on Thursday last week.

The Viva refinery and the Ampol-owned Lytton refinery in Brisbane each provide about 10 per cent of Australia's fuel.

The remainder is imported from overseas.

The Geelong refinery, according to Viva Energy, can process up to 120,000 barrels of oil per day — manufacturing petrol, diesel, LPG, jet fuel and more.

Refinery down to 60 per cent

The fire has impaired production capacity at the refinery, now operating at 60 per cent for petrol and 80 per cent for the production of diesel and jet fuel.

"It allows us to minimise the number of units in operation, particularly around where the incident occurred," Mr Wyatt said.

"And so it's a kind of a safe operating parameter at this current time.

"As we get access to the area, we have to inspect the units that will allow us to restart and get close to over 90 per cent of our production capability."

Inspection of areas potentially indirectly affected is still needed to ensure they are safe to restart, he said, adding that the process would happen over the next few weeks.

The cause of the Viva Energy oil refinery fire under investigation. Here's what we know Firefighters have managed to extinguish a blaze at one of Australia's major oil refineries. Here's what we know so far about the cause of the fire — and the possible impact on fuel prices.

Mr Wyatt said he did not expect the fire to cause any long-term damage to the refinery's output, including premium fuel.

"The majority of what we produce at Geelong will continue unaffected once we've brought all the units back up to their normal capacity," he said.

Less crude to go around

Oil prices have gone up about $30 a barrel since the beginning of the Iran war on February 28.

The cost of buying diesel and jet fuel from the region has gone up by about $120 a barrel, representing the huge demand for those products.

Petrol has gone up by about $50 a barrel.

Loading...

"[It reflects] the demand for gasoline is not as strong as it is for jet fuel and diesel, which are the engine room of the economy, really within the Asia-Pacific region," Mr Wyatt said.

He said Viva Energy Australia had faced a tough operating environment for years.

"I mean, the majority of the cost of fuel is represented by the 80 per cent of [oil] that's being imported," Mr Wyatt said.

"I think we all want refineries to continue to be part of the Australian energy security mix, and to do that, the refineries need to be profitable, and they need to make money to obviously continue to run sustainably and make the investments that we need, both in running a safe and efficient operation, but also continue to invest for the future.

"We've just come out of a program late last year of upgrading the refinery to produce low-sulphur fuel; so, much cleaner fuel for the environment in Australia.

" All those investments are not possible without, obviously, a profitable business and, obviously, the support that we get from government from time to time through the fuel security services payment. "

More refineries needed for secure supply

The fire at Viva's Geelong refinery highlighted threats to Australia's fuel security, which Mr Wyatt said had been adequate until now.

"We have two refineries that are playing a really important role today," he said.

"Making 20 per cent of Australia's requirements is not insignificant."

But more would be good, he said.

"I don't think … anyone wants to live through this again … [to] have the level of insecurity that we feel at the moment," he said.

"And obviously if you build new, you'll be building more modern refineries.

" We can also add capacity to the refineries we have, but we can also build storage. "

Strait of Hormuz

Australia's refining capacity would not be in the headlines if not for the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

Mr Wyatt considers the crisis a week-by-week situation.

The battle over the Strait of Hormuz By moving so much of the war into the Strait of Hormuz and Persian Gulf, Tehran has hit its adversaries where it hurts the most and analysts warn that while the United States military is mighty, history shows in asymmetrical warfare, the lesser power can win the day.

"[We're typically] buying fuel six weeks in advance, so we're into June now [and] every week we're able to do that is another good week," he said.

"It gives us another week to see a resolution to the conflict and then a resolution to the normal flows of oil and refined products that we all rely on."

But a crunch point for fuel supply remains a risk.

"There's still 80-85 per cent of the oil that's still flowing, and refineries are still operating, and there is still fuel available, so it's not like there's a cliff out there that we're sailing into,' Mr Wyatt said.

World.title: 'Finfluencers' suspected of giving unlawful advice hit with warning notices
World.content:
Four Australian influencers have been hit with warning notices from the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) — accused of "misleading and deceptive conduct".

The warning notice to the so-called "finfluencers" related to suspected provision of unlicensed financial advice, including promoting claims of guaranteed returns.

A guaranteed return, which ASIC deemed misleading, is the promise a financial investment will bring in a set income.

Spotting bad money advice online Did you know if someone gives financial advice without a licence, they could face hefty fines and up to five years in prison?

The notice sent to the four advised them to "carefully consider" ASIC's guidance, noting they should seek their own legal advice.

"ASIC is concerned that you may be contravening Australian financial services laws by carrying on a financial services business in Australia without being authorised to do so," the letter said.

"It is your responsibility to be aware of and comply with your obligations."

The notice was the first time since it published guidance for online financial services in 2022 that ASIC has nudged licensees regarding their obligations.

Unlicensed influencers are allowed to operate as authorised representatives of Australian Financial Services (AFS) licensees — but the licensees are responsible for what they say and do.

ASIC has also commenced a review of several AFS licensees and their supervision of 15 finfluencers operating under their licences.

Global push

The ongoing crackdown comes in the second Global Week of Action Against Unlawful Finfluencers, an event involving 17 global regulators.

Loading...

Finfluencer activity in Australia, according to ASIC Commissioner Alan Kirkland, is "significant".

"That's not a concern to us if finfluencers are operating within the law, but we are particularly concerned if they're giving financial advice," he said.

"Because if influencers are encouraging people to invest their money in particular ways, then that carries risks for those investors.

" This is an issue of global concern. "

ASIC, Mr Kirkland noted, was actively monitoring social media to identify finfluencer activity which may breach the law.

"We also get valuable reports from members of the public where they see things that they think may not be right," he said.

"It's based on those sources of intelligence that we've identified some influencers that we think may be breaking the law, and they're the ones that we've issued warning notices to."

Influencers 'promising fast or easy money' on social media

ASIC has previously taken action against licensees who fail to properly supervise their finfluencers.

In February it cancelled the AFS licence of a company who failed to ensure its representatives were complying with the law.

ASIC's finfluencer red flags: Promises of fast, easy money

Personality over substance — using confidence to build 'instant trust'

Hyperbolic claims of success with no detail or downsides

No clear licensing or credentials, making advice hard to verify

Urgency/pressure, encouraging quick decisions

Free content funnelling followers into paid groups

In 2022, another ASIC crackdown left finfluencers scrambling to take down posts and others abandoning their platforms altogether.

At that time, the regulator made it clear they could face jail time or fines of more than $1 million for talking about stocks, investment funds or financial products.

This latest crackdown, according to ASIC, reflected its concern about the influence of social media on financial decision-making.

"We often see finfluencers promising fast or easy money, often associated with the allure of a lavish lifestyle," Mr Kirkland said.

"Often there's a real emphasis on … the power of the personality of the finfluencer that obscures the lack of substance in their advice.

" And there's often a sense of urgency that they create, the sense that unless you act now, you're going to miss out on this great opportunity. "

"Any of those signs are red flags."

AI is not always '100pc accurate' but some still use it for financial advice When Georgina Doll was looking to buy a home, generative artificial intelligence was one of the sources she turned to for advice.

Those 2022 guidelines published by ASIC were a "turning point", according to Angel Zhong, the deputy dean of Research and Innovation and RMIT University's School of Economics, Finance and Marketing.

"I've been checking several high profile finfluencers in Australia," she said.

"Since that regulatory guidance in 2022, some of them actually ceased being influencers, and some of them actually went on and obtained licenses.

"To some extent, it worked, however the whole ecosystem hasn't disappeared."

Her advice to someone looking at finfluencer content was simple: "There is never a free lunch."

" Treat financial advice from social media the way you would treat a diet tip from a stranger at the gym. "

"It could be interesting [but] it may not be tailored to you because individual financial circumstances differ."

63 per cent of Gen Z using social media for financial advice

An estimated 63 per cent of Gen Z Australians — aged 18-28 — rely on their social media for financial information, according to ASIC's Gen Z Financial Behaviours Report published last month.

Three in ten (30 per cent) told the regulator they used YouTube for financial advice, while 19 per cent used Instagram, 17 per cent used TikTok and 18 per cent used AI platforms.

One in 10 relied on online finfluencers.

Dr Dimitrios Sampasis, an associate professor of Emerging Technologies and FinTech, said finfluencers were likely filling a gap in the market.

"Their audience would be people who normally wouldn't be able to access proper financial advice, probably because of the cost," he told the ABC.

Families search online for financial advice Financial advisors are urging caution for people turning to social media for financial advice as cost-of-living increases squeeze budgets.

"Or [it's] because people want someone to provide simplistic or simplified explanations of complex topics."

Referencing ASIC's Gen Z report, he noted consuming financial content was "a matter of trust".

"It's a matter of trusting what you actually see," he said.

"Often photos or visuals speak louder than words, so it's interesting to see … especially now in the time of AI, we're looking at 30 per cent of [Gen Z] would be using YouTube specifically.

"This is all creating a new narrative, a new generation of people looking into the traditional finfluencer.

"Unfortunately we have been seeing lots of cases [where it's] a lack of financial literacy, specifically people falling into different scams and fraudulent activities.

"And I'm not connecting the two, but definitely the financial literacy part is a bigger picture, which also includes [people knowing] where you actually go and look for this kind of financial advice, or simply looking into potential financial information."

Financial literacy 'the elephant in the room'

While international coordination was "key" to policing the social media space, Ms Zhong there was still more work to do.

"The elephant in the room is the lack of financial literacy," she said.

"Why do people turn to influencers in the first place? The whole thing elevated during COVID, at that time we had a lot of first-time investors in Australia and around the globe.

"If everyone is equipped with the same amount of financial literacy, they may not need to rely upon influencers so heavily.

"Or they may, but they'll be able to judge whether this particular advice is dodgy or appropriate."

Loading...

One potential solution, according to Dr Sampasis, was creating a list of "accredited finfluencers".

"I think having … licensed ones that people can trust, who will comply with the law, is very important," he said.

"There you actually have a reference point … you can look at and say, 'OK, these people have been authorised, these people can be trusted'.

"That [would mean] they have gone through specific due diligence, they have gone through specific criteria, they have gone through specific checking.

Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders voted overwhelmingly to approve a merger with Paramount Skydance, despite widespread opposition to the deal in Hollywood.

Paramount agreed to buy Warner Bros. for $US110 billion ($151 billion) in February, beating out Netflix after a months-long bidding war. Stakeholders are set to receive $US31 in cash for each share of Warner Bros. common stock that they own once the agreement goes through.

Warner Bros. Discovery CEO David Zaslav. Bloomberg

The deal is still facing antitrust review in several jurisdictions, including the US and EU. If it has not been finalised by September 30, they will receive 25 cents per share for each quarter until closing as part of a “ticking fee.”

“We look forward to closing the transaction in the coming months and realising the creation of a next-generation media and entertainment company that better serves both the creative community and consumers,” a spokesperson for Paramount said in a statement.

World.title: Bulldogs escape injury catastrophe, but their nightmare hasn’t ended
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Bulldogs escape injury catastrophe, but their nightmare hasn’t ended Andrew Wu April 24, 2026 — 1:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

Loading

The Western Bulldogs are optimistic Aaron Naughton has avoided serious damage to his neck after a sickening fall in their 11-goal drubbing to Sydney, but the club’s injury crisis has worsened. Naughton will undergo scans on his neck on Friday and, though he showed no early signs of concussion immediately after the Dogs’ latest thumping at Marvel Stadium, he is in doubt to face Fremantle next week. Loading The Dogs were dealt another setback with key defender Rory Lobb’s hamstring injury worse than initially thought – and set to rule him out for a month – while ruckman Tim English is expected to miss at least another match. On top of the ladder just over a fortnight ago, the injury-ravaged Dogs are a shadow of the side that was the last team to taste defeat this season, and have now lost their past three games by a total of 181 points.



Aaron Naughton was cleared of serious injury after a sickening fall in the Bulldogs’ loss to Sydney. AFL Photos The Swans capitalised on the massive holes created by the Bulldogs’ injuries. A week after Geelong star Jeremy Cameron slammed home 10 goals against their undermanned defence, missing Lobb and James O’Donnell, Charlie Curnow and Joel Amartey booted seven goals and three respectively. The pair were far too good for the undersized Buku Khamis and Ryan Gardner, the latter playing just his second senior game since late 2023. Ruckman Brodie Grundy capitalised on English’s absence with 35 hitouts, 18 possessions and two goals in a starring performance.



View post on X Naughton landed on his head and neck after flipping midair attempting a high mark on Jai Serong deep in the Bulldogs’ forward line in the third quarter. He was tended to by medical staff, who placed a brace around his neck, before he was driven down the race into the rooms on a motorised stretcher. He was walking in the rooms and not wearing a brace after the game, but was expected to spend Thursday night with his parents. Charlie Curnow celebrates one of his seven goals. AFL Photos “He’s gonna go home now, and he’ll have his neck looked at tomorrow and [we’ll] get back to you on it,” Bulldogs coach Luke Beveridge said. “He appears to have strained down that side of his neck from the incident.



“The bright side is there are no signs of concussion, but we’ll have to report in once we get something more definitive from a scan.” Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 ‘Bordering on bullying’: Blues hand their report to AFL as Voss hits back at critics over Hollands matter Naughton’s injury comes a week after Sam Darcy suffered a season-ending anterior cruciate ligament tear. Without their twin towers in attack, the Dogs finished the game with a pair of third-gamers Will Lewis and Louis Emmett filling the key forward posts. The Dogs had harboured hope Lobb would be available to face the Swans, but he felt sore in another part of his hamstring at training during the week and was sent for more scans, which revealed a more serious injury. “Something showed up as a bit risky, and so we’ll need to be conservative with him,” Beveridge said.



“The initial signs were that he got a knock, [and] bit of bleeding, probably from that. But then subsequently, in another spot, he had some discomfort so we went out to look at that, and it showed up something that could turn into something worse. He’ll be out for a good month as well.” Beveridge said English did not move well at training “so I wouldn’t think that he’s available next week”. Western Bulldogs captain Marcus Bontempelli leads his team onto the field. Getty Images The Bulldogs made a fast start with the first three goals of the game, and trailed by only 13 points at the long break but were steamrolled in the second half. Skipper Marcus Bontempelli addressed the players in the rooms for about five minutes after the game – on the night he and his 2016 premiership teammates were to celebrate the 10-year reunion from that year’s triumph over Sydney. He was visibly frustrated during the game on Thursday night and had an animated discussion with Matt Kennedy on the field after the half-time siren, and was also vocal as he led his players off the field for the break.



Kennedy (15 disposals) and Ed Richards (18) were among the senior Dogs who had off nights. Related Article AFL 2026 AFL round seven teams and expert tips: Reinforcements arrive for Magpies, but skipper still missing “He’s an influencer, he’s an authority, he’s a powerful character, and he wants to take people with him,” Beveridge said of his captain. “His expectations are high, no matter who’s playing with him. “He wants things now, and he’s pushing to get it. We all need to understand what we can influence and control, and he’s working through that in his own leadership capacity. “He’s always a tremendous support for his teammates, but on nights like this, there was always going to be an element of frustration with everything, with everyone, and he’s probably feeling a fair bit of that.”



Injuries to their stars have exposed the depth on the Dogs’ list, forcing Beveridge to play eight players with fewer than 15 games’ experience. Editor's pick Opinion

AFL 2026 Yze can coach, but he can’t do it with one hand tied behind his back Jimmy Bartel Age columnist, Brownlow and Norm Smith medallist He has the difficult task of convincing young pups like Jedd Busslinger, Lewis and Emmett they can contribute to Bulldogs victories while knowing full well his team is significantly weakened by their lengthy injury list. “I think it’s the two c-words – capacity and capability,” Beveridge said. “We’ve got a lot of boys who haven’t played a lot of footy yet, and they’re just finding out what AFL footy is about. “Form ends up being linked to those things.



“And sometimes that’s linked to inexperience. You still need your more experienced players to give you a bit more of a chance, and we just didn’t quite have enough influence there tonight.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Api Koroisau could be in trouble for two tackles in potential blow for Tigers and Blues
World.content:
Wests Tigers 33 Canberra 14 SportNRLNRL 2026 Api Koroisau could be in trouble for two tackles in potential blow for Tigers and Blues Christian Nicolussi Updated April 23, 2026 — 11:48pm ,first published 10:07pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

Leichhardt Oval: Wests Tigers will be sweating on Api Koroisau being cleared of a hip-drop tackle and a dangerous throw that could also threaten NSW Origin’s preparations. Koroisau was sin-binned approaching the half-hour mark on Thursday night when he came down on the back of Canberra back-rower Noah Martin’s leg. Loading Martin yelled out in pain, stayed on the field, but spent most of the second half watching from the bench. The Raiders raced in two tries while Koroisau was on the sidelines.



Should the match review committee charge Koroisau on Friday morning, he will be hoping for nothing more than a grade-one dangerous contact charge, which carries a $3000 fine. A grade-two dangerous contact charge, however, will mean a three-match ban. Koroisau has already been charged three times with dangerous contact. Will Api Koroisau be in trouble for this tackle? Nine Then in the 53rd minute, Koroisau was placed on report a second time for a lifting tackle on Morgan Smithies. If charged with a grade-one dangerous throw, Koroisau will face a two-match ban. Any time out of the game would be a huge blow for the Tigers who meet Cronulla, Melbourne, then Manly at Magic Round.



A minimum three-match ban also means Koroisau would not play again before Origin I. Koroisau is in contention for a NSW recall after Penrith hooker Mitch Kenny was ruled out for up to three months with a broken leg. Tigers coach Benji Marshall was at a loss to explain why Koroisau had been sanctioned for either tackle, especially the alleged hip-drop. “It’s probably not a good time, but who cares – the inconsistency with the refereeing is annoying me at the moment,” Marshall said. “I know we won, but some of the calls … it’s hard to understand. Even Api’s case with the sin-bin, I don’t know what he’s supposed to do in that situation. He’s making a cover tackle from behind, where he has to tackle his legs, and that’s where he’s going to end up. “I don’t think it was intentional. He did his ten minutes, surely that’s enough.“



“I think the fans deserve some consistency around interpretations of the rules. We’re not getting it.” As for the lifting tackle, Marshall said: “If it was up to me, I probably would have challenged it [the penalty]. I didn’t think it was that bad.” Koroisau was excellent for most of the night and was unlucky not to receive a penalty of his own when he appeared to be kicked in the face by Ethan Sanders midway through the second half. Adam Doueihi celebrates scoring his first try of the night against Canberra. NRL Images The Tigers raced to a 10-0 lead at a packed Leichhardt Oval – the official count was 17,153 – with tries to Luke Laulilii and Adam Doueihi. Laulilii pounced on a wobbly Koroisau kick in the left corner.



The Raiders, already missing Simi Sasagi and Josh Papalii to injury, as well as the suspended Hudson Young, looked in serious trouble when Ethan Strange hobbled from the field in the opening 10 minutes. He received a painkilling injection into his ankle, and was able to return before the break. Related Article NRL 2026 Tigers send sold-out Leichhardt crowd into frenzy with Raiders rout The best moment of the night took place in the 46th minute when Jarome Luai put Samuela Fainu into a hole, then the giant back-rower hit and spun out of a tackle before squeezing a pass for Doueihi to score his second try. The second-best moment was when Doueihi looked ready to collect a hat-trick of tries, only for Kaeo Weekes to produce a belter of a tackle as the last line of defence. The third-best moment was the sight of big Royce Hunt showing serious speed to score the final try. Who knew the big fella could move so quickly.



As for Doueihi, fans should make a point of re-reading Andrew Johns’ Thursday column in the Herald about why the Tigers’ fan favourite would be an ideal No. 14 for the Blues. The Tigers’ Mr Fix-It gets better each week. Form back-rower Kai Pearce-Paul failed a head injury assessment, which means he is now unavailable next week, while Jahream Bula came from the field in the final 10 minutes with a shoulder injury. He received a rock-star reception as he walked back to the bench in front of the main grandstand. The Tigers head to Cronulla next Sunday while Canberra take on the Gold Coast. World.title: ‘He smacked me’: An insight into Charlie Curnow’s dominance as Swans destroy Bulldogs at Marvel
World.content:
The Western Bulldogs’ injury crisis has claimed another star player with key forward Aaron Naughton stretchered off the ground after a sickening fall in the club’s defeat to Sydney on Thursday night.

The Swans’ star recruit Charlie Curnow feasted on the Dogs’ undermanned defence to boot seven goals on another dirty night for Luke Beveridge’s decimated team, who were no match after half-time to lose by 66 points – 18.18 (126) to 9.6 (60).

Charlie Curnow takes possession ahead of Buku Khamis. AFL Photos

On top of the ladder just over a fortnight ago, the Dogs are a shadow of the side that was the last team to taste defeat this season and have now lost their past three games by a combined total of 181 points.

This loss, on the night they celebrated the 10-year reunion of their fairytale 2016 flag, was compounded by a terrifying incident involving Naughton.

Naughton landed on his head after flipping midair, attempting a high mark on Jai Serong deep in the Bulldogs’ forward line.

Aaron Naughton is treated by medical staff after his horror fall. AFL Photos

The Dog have cleared Naughton of serious injury, but he is in extreme doubt for the Dogs’ clash with leading premiership fancy Fremantle on Friday week.

“Initial examination makes us optimistic that Aaron has avoided any serious injuries,” the Bulldogs said in a statement released in the final quarter.

“He will be reassessed over the coming days.”

The injury is another devastating blow to the Dogs, who last week lost the other half of their star forward pairing Sam Darcy to a season-ending knee injury. Ruckman Tim English and key defenders James O’Donnell and Rory Lobb are also on a lengthy injury list.

The Dogs finished the game with young pups Louis Emmett and Will Lewis deep in attack.

The absences of O’Donnell and Lobb were keenly felt. Curnow and Joel Amartey combined for Sydney’s first eight goals and finished with 10 of their side’s 18.

World.title: Trump orders navy to ‘shoot and kill’ mine-laying boats in Strait of Hormuz
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastMiddle East at war Trump orders navy to ‘shoot and kill’ mine-laying boats in Strait of Hormuz Updated April 23, 2026 — 11:10pm ,first published 5:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

US President Donald Trump said he had ordered the navy to “shoot and kill” any boats laying mines in the Strait of Hormuz after Iran seized two ships and tightened its grip on the strategic waterway during an indefinite ceasefire with no sign of peace talks restarting. “I have ordered the United States Navy to shoot and kill any boat, small boats though they may be (Their naval ships are ALL, 159 of them, at the bottom of the sea!), that is putting mines in the waters of the Strait of Hormuz,” Trump said in a post on Truth Social on Thursday. “There is to be no hesitation. Additionally, our mine ‘sweepers’ are clearing the Strait right now. I am hereby ordering that activity to continue, but at a tripled up level!” Ships lie at anchor off the major Iranian port of Bandar Abbas, which is under blockade by the US Navy. Getty Images In a separate post, Trump claimed the US had “total control over the Strait of Hormuz” and that no ship could enter or leave without the approval of the navy. “It is ‘Sealed up Tight,’ until such time as Iran is able to make a DEAL!!!” he said.



The status of a two-week-old ceasefire, due to expire earlier this week, has remained unclear. In a sharp about-face hours after threatening renewed violence, Trump made what appeared to be a unilateral announcement that the US would extend the truce until it had discussed an Iranian proposal in peace talks to end the two-month-old war. But Iranian officials did not say they had agreed to any ceasefire extension and criticised Trump’s decision to maintain the US blockade of Iran’s ports, itself considered by Tehran as an act of war. Related Article Middle East at war Iran claims it has seized two ships after Trump extended ceasefire indefinitely Iran’s ​parliament Speaker, and lead negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said a full ceasefire only made sense if the blockade was lifted. Reopening the Strait of Hormuz, the strategic waterway that carried a fifth of the world’s oil trade before the war, was impossible with such a “flagrant breach of the ceasefire”, Ghalibaf said on social media.



“You did not achieve your goals through military aggression, and you will not achieve them by bullying either,” he wrote in his first response to Trump’s announcement. “The only way is recognising the Iranian people’s rights.” Trump again backed away at the last moment from his repeated threats to bomb Iran’s power plants and other civilian infrastructure, which the United Nations and others have warned would violate international humanitarian law. But little progress has been made in ending the war that started with joint US-Israeli attacks on Iran on February 28. That leaves the two sides in a holding pattern, with the Strait of Hormuz effectively closed, straining economies worldwide. Iranian state television reported Iran’s paramilitary Revolutionary Guard had seized two ships – identified as the MSC Francesca and the Epaminondas – after three vessels were attacked in the strait on Wednesday. The two ships were reportedly being taken to Iran for “inspection of their cargo, documents, and records”. The third vessel, a Liberian-flagged container ship, was fired on in the same area but was not damaged and resumed sailing, according to maritime security sources.



White House spokesperson Karoline Leavitt told Fox News that since the ships were not US or Israeli vessels, the seizure was not a violation of the ceasefire. She called it an act of “piracy”. Loading Traffic through the strait ground to a halt following the seizures. Only one ship, bulk carrier LB Energy, was seen moving through the waterway early on Thursday, with none observed entering. The tanker Ocean Jewel is currently idling at the entrance to the corridor, having aborted a transit not long after Iranian forces began firing at three ships. The US military said on Wednesday it had so far directed more than 30 ships to turn around or return to port as part of its blockade against Iran. Far beyond the Gulf, the US has intercepted at least three Iranian-flagged tankers in Asian waters, sources said, redirecting them away from their positions near India, Malaysia and Sri Lanka. Brent, the international crude oil benchmark, remained above $US100 a barrel in Asian trade on Thursday, having hit triple figures a day earlier for the first time in two weeks.



No new deadline In his Tuesday announcement, Trump said he had agreed to a request by Pakistani mediators “to hold our Attack on the Country of Iran until such time as their leaders and representatives can come up with a unified proposal ... and discussions are concluded, one way or the other” Trump has declined to set an expiry date on the ceasefire. AP He has not set any deadline for the proposal or discussions, Leavitt told reporters. Pakistan, which has acted as a mediator, was still trying to bring the sides together after both failed to show up for tentatively scheduled talks in Islamabad on Tuesday before the two-week-old ceasefire was due to expire.



A first session of peace talks between Iran and the US in Islamabad 11 days ago produced no agreement. Trump wants Iran to give up highly enriched uranium and forgo further enrichment to prevent it from building a nuclear weapon. Iran says it has only a peaceful civilian nuclear programme, and wants the lifting of sanctions, reparations for damage and recognition of its control over the strait. Related Article Analysis

Middle East at war Trump’s Iran deal may need him to do the unthinkable Iran has also made a ceasefire between Israel and Lebanon’s Hezbollah militant group a condition of truce talks. On Wednesday, Israeli air strikes on Lebanon killed at least five people, including the Lebanese journalist Amal Khalil, in the deadliest day since a 10-day ceasefire was announced on April 16. On the eve of further talks in Washington between Lebanese and Israeli ambassadors on Thursday, Lebanese President Joseph Aoun said Beirut would seek an extension to the ceasefire, which is set to expire on Sunday.



Thousands of people have been killed across the Middle East, mostly in Iran and Lebanon. Reuters Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.
